mcqs.question: How does BERT produce different vectors for "bank" in "river bank" versus "bank" in "bank loan", given both start from the identical input token?
options: BERT stores a separate lookup table entry for each meaning of "bank" ahead of time
Self-attention layers compute each token's output from its surrounding context at inference time, so different neighboring words produce different final vectors for the same input token
BERT runs a separate sense-disambiguation classifier before the main model
The tokenizer splits "bank" differently depending on the sentence
mcqs.explanation: The token embedding for "bank" starts identical in both sentences, but self-attention recomputes each token's representation using its actual surrounding context, so the layers pull in different neighboring information ("river" vs "loan") and produce different output vectors. There's no pre-built sense lookup (A), no separate disambiguation model (C), and subword tokenization of "bank" doesn't change based on sentence content (D).

mcqs.question: Why must BERT's Masked Language Modeling objective use bidirectional context, unlike a standard next-token prediction objective?
options: Because predicting a masked token in the middle of a sentence requires information from both the words before and after it, which forces the model to build bidirectional representations
Because bidirectional context reduces the total training time compared to left-to-right prediction
Because masked tokens are always at the start of the sequence, requiring only right-context
Bidirectionality is an implementation detail unrelated to the MLM objective itself
mcqs.explanation: MLM masks random tokens anywhere in the sequence, and correctly predicting them typically requires looking at words on both sides — a next-token (left-to-right only) objective couldn't use this signal fully, which is exactly why MLM is designed to force bidirectional representation learning. It's not about training speed (B), masked tokens are scattered throughout the sequence, not just at the start (C), and bidirectionality is central to the objective's design, not incidental (D).

mcqs.question: You need to fine-tune BERT for Named Entity Recognition. How does the task head differ from a text-classification head?
options: NER requires no task head at all — pretrained BERT already outputs entity labels

A classification head applies one linear layer to the `[CLS]` token; an NER head applies a linear layer to every token's representation, since NER predicts a label per token (sequence labeling), not one label per input
NER requires retraining the entire model from random initialization, unlike classification
NER uses next-sentence prediction directly as its objective
mcqs.explanation: The structural difference comes from what's being predicted: classification needs one label for the whole input, so it reads only the pooled `[CLS]` representation; NER needs a label per token, so the head is applied token-wise across the whole sequence. Pretrained BERT doesn't emit entity labels without a task head (A is false), fine-tuning starts from pretrained weights, not random initialization (C is false), and NSP is a pretraining objective unrelated to the NER fine-tuning head (D is a category error).

mcqs.question: Why can't GPT be pretrained with BERT's Masked Language Modeling objective without changing its use case?
options: GPT's causal (left-to-right) attention mask prevents any token from seeing future tokens, which is required for MLM's bidirectional prediction but is exactly what GPT needs to avoid for valid autoregressive generation at inference time
GPT does not use subword tokenization, making masking incompatible
MLM only works on classification datasets, and GPT is never used for classification
GPT has no attention mechanism at all, only feedforward layers
mcqs.explanation: The masking difference is architectural and deliberate: GPT's causal mask blocks each position from attending to future tokens, which is precisely what makes it a valid autoregressive generator (at inference, future tokens genuinely don't exist yet). Training it with a bidirectional MLM objective would contradict this causal structure. GPT does use subword tokenization (B is false), MLM's applicability isn't limited to classification datasets (C is false), and GPT absolutely uses self-attention, just causally masked (D is false).

mcqs.question: A team pools raw off-the-shelf BERT `[CLS]` embeddings to build a semantic search index and finds similarity rankings are mediocre. What is the most likely explanation?
options: BERT embeddings are too low-dimensional to represent semantic similarity

Vanilla BERT was pretrained with masked-language and next-sentence objectives, not a similarity objective, so its raw `[CLS]` output isn't optimized for ranking sentence similarity — models fine-tuned specifically for sentence embeddings perform far better
Semantic search requires a decoder-only model, and BERT is encoder-only
The `[CLS]` token only stores positional information, not semantic content
mcqs.explanation: This is a known, practically important caveat: off-the-shelf BERT was never trained to make similar sentences produce nearby `[CLS]` vectors — that requires an explicit fine-tuning step (e.g. Sentence-BERT) with a similarity-aware objective. Dimensionality isn't the bottleneck (A), semantic search works fine with encoder-only models when properly fine-tuned (C is false), and `[CLS]` does carry semantic content, just not similarity-optimized content by default (D is false).

mcqs.question: A company needs to classify support tickets into 20 fixed categories, with thousands of labeled examples available and a need for low-latency, low-cost inference. Which approach best fits, per the encoder-only vs decoder-only trade-off?
options: Prompt a large decoder-only LLM per ticket, since it requires no training data

Fine-tune a small encoder-only model (like BERT) with a classification head, since it's a fixed-input, fixed-label understanding task with ample labeled data, and encoder-only models are cheaper and faster at inference
Encoder-only models cannot be used for classification tasks at all
The choice makes no practical difference in cost or latency
mcqs.explanation: This is exactly the understanding-task scenario encoder-only models are built for: a fixed input, a fixed label set, and enough labeled data to fine-tune — a small BERT-class model will typically match or beat a large LLM's prompted accuracy at a fraction of the inference cost and latency. Prompting an LLM (A) works but is usually more expensive and slower per ticket at scale; encoder-only models are commonly used for classification, that's their primary use case (C is false); cost and latency differences between the two approaches are often substantial at scale (D is false).
